title: Muscle & Nervous Tissue
summary: Complete the four tissue types by learning how contractile and excitable tissues look and are built.

lessons.title: Skeletal Muscle & the Sarcomere

levels.kid:
Make a muscle with your arm. Inside it are long, thin cells called **muscle fibers**. They are so long that one cell can stretch a big part of the way along a muscle!

Under a microscope, these fibers look striped, like a zebra. The stripes come from tiny repeating boxes called **sarcomeres**. Each box holds thin threads and thick threads lying side by side.

When your brain says "move!", the thick threads grab the thin threads and pull them inward, like hands pulling a rope. Every box gets a little shorter. Millions of boxes shortening together make your whole muscle pull.

The fuel for this pulling is a special energy molecule called **ATP**. Your muscles use lots of it when you run and play.
levels.hs:
**Skeletal muscle** is the muscle attached to bones that you control on purpose. Its cells, called **muscle fibers**, are unusual: each one forms when many smaller cells fuse together during development. That gives every fiber many **nuclei**, pushed to the edge of the cell just under its membrane (the **sarcolemma**).

Under a light microscope, skeletal muscle shows **striations**, alternating dark and light bands:
- **A band** (dark): the length of the thick filaments, made of the protein **myosin**.
- **I band** (light): the region with only thin filaments, made mostly of **actin**.
- **Z line** (or Z disc): a thin dark line in the middle of each I band.

The stretch from one Z line to the next is a **sarcomere**, the basic contractile unit. It is about 2-3 micrometers long at rest.

Muscle contracts by the **sliding filament mechanism**: myosin heads bind actin, pull, let go and grab again, using ATP. The thin filaments slide toward the center of the sarcomere. The filaments themselves do not get shorter. Instead, the I band and the central H zone narrow while the A band stays the same width.

Think of a sprinter: millions of sarcomeres in the thigh muscles shorten at the same instant to push off the blocks.
levels.college:
**Organization.** A whole muscle is wrapped in **epimysium**. Bundles of fibers (**fascicles**) are wrapped in **perimysium**, and each fiber is surrounded by **endomysium**, a thin layer of reticular fibers and basal lamina carrying capillaries. Fibers are multinucleated syncytia (10-100 µm wide, up to many centimeters long) with peripheral nuclei. **Satellite cells**, muscle stem cells, sit between the sarcolemma and the basal lamina.

**Bands of the sarcomere** (Z line to Z line):
- **A band**: the thick myosin filaments plus overlapping actin. It is anisotropic, meaning it looks bright under polarized light.
- **H zone**: the central part of the A band where there is no actin overlap. Its center is the **M line**, where proteins such as myomesin crosslink the thick filaments.
- **I band**: thin filaments only. It is isotropic, and the Z disc bisects it.
- **Z disc**: contains **α-actinin**, which anchors the barbed ends of the actin filaments.

In cross-section through the overlap zone, each thick filament is surrounded by six thin filaments in a hexagonal lattice.

**Excitation-contraction coupling.** Invaginations of the sarcolemma called **T-tubules** sit at the A-I junction. In mammals that gives two per sarcomere. Each T-tubule is flanked by two terminal cisternae of the **sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)**, and together they form a **triad**. Depolarization is sensed by **dihydropyridine receptors** (Cav1.1), which mechanically open **ryanodine receptors (RyR1)** in the SR. Ca2+ is released and binds **troponin C**, which shifts **tropomyosin** off myosin-binding sites on actin. Cross-bridges then cycle. **SERCA** pumps return Ca2+ to the SR so the muscle can relax.

**Fiber types.**
- **Type I** (slow oxidative): rich in myoglobin and mitochondria, so they look red.
- **Type IIa** (fast oxidative-glycolytic).
- **Type IIx/IIb** (fast glycolytic): pale.

Histochemistry, such as myosin ATPase or NADH-TR staining, reveals a checkerboard mosaic of fiber types within a single muscle.
levels.phd:
The sliding filament theory came from two 1954 *Nature* papers published side by side. A.F. Huxley and Niedergerke used interference microscopy, and H.E. Huxley and Hanson used phase-contrast and electron microscopy. Both showed that the A band stays constant while the I band and H zone shorten. In 1966, Gordon, Huxley and Julian produced the **length-tension relationship**. They found that active force falls linearly as filament overlap decreases beyond about 2.2 µm, reaching zero near 3.6 µm in frog fibers. This tied force directly to the number of available cross-bridges. The plateau occurs at about 2.0-2.2 µm, where every myosin head in the overlap zone can reach actin.

**Cross-bridge cycle** (Lymn-Taylor, 1971):
- ATP binding detaches the myosin head from actin.
- Hydrolysis to ADP + Pi recocks the lever arm.
- The head binds weakly, then strongly, to actin.
- Pi release triggers the power stroke, a working stroke of about 5-10 nm.
- ADP release leaves the rigor state, which persists in rigor mortis when ATP is absent.

Rayment's 1993 crystal structure of the myosin S1 fragment supported a swinging lever-arm model.

**The third and fourth filaments.**
- **Titin**, the largest known protein (about 3-4 MDa), spans half a sarcomere from the Z disc to the M line. Its PEVK and tandem-Ig segments act as a molecular spring that generates passive tension and keeps the thick filament centered.
- **Nebulin** runs along the thin filaments and helps specify their length. Capping proteins anchor the filament ends: CapZ at the barbed end and tropomodulin at the pointed end.

**Regulation.** Tropomyosin occupies three states, blocked, closed and open, described by McKillop and Geeves. Ca2+ binding to troponin C shifts the equilibrium toward the closed state, and strong myosin binding then pushes it to the open state. This cooperativity yields steep force-pCa curves.

Skeletal muscle's DHPR-RyR1 link is mechanical and does not depend on Ca2+ influx. Cardiac muscle instead uses calcium-induced calcium release.

**Costameres** connect the Z discs to the sarcolemma and on to the extracellular matrix. They do this through the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex and integrins, transmitting force laterally across the fiber.
levels.expert:
In the clinic, skeletal muscle histology is read from a **muscle biopsy**, usually from the vastus lateralis or deltoid. The specimen is snap-frozen in isopentane cooled by liquid nitrogen. Formalin fixation introduces artifacts and destroys the enzyme activity needed for histochemistry.

The core panel:
- **H&E**: fiber size variation, nuclei that have moved into the fiber center, necrosis and inflammation.
- **Modified Gomori trichrome**: **ragged-red fibers**, from subsarcolemmal mitochondrial accumulation in mitochondrial myopathies, and the rods of nemaline myopathy.
- **NADH-TR, SDH and COX**: COX-negative/SDH-positive fibers support a mitochondrial DNA defect.
- **ATPase at pH 9.4, 4.6 and 4.3**: fiber typing.

**Patterns are the payoff.**
- **Fiber-type grouping**, where large patches are all one type, signals denervation followed by reinnervation.
- **Small angular fibers** indicate active denervation.
- **Myopathic patterns** show rounded fibers of varied size, internalized nuclei, necrosis and regeneration. Regenerating fibers are basophilic and express neonatal myosin.
- **Perifascicular atrophy** points to dermatomyositis.

**Mutations in sarcomere and associated proteins** produce defined diseases:
- Loss of dystrophin, confirmed by immunostaining or Western blot, causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- Nebulin (NEB) and ACTA1 mutations cause nemaline myopathy.
- Truncating titin (TTN) variants underlie some dilated cardiomyopathy and distal titinopathies.
- RYR1 variants cause central core disease and **malignant hyperthermia susceptibility**. In susceptible people, volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine trigger uncontrolled SR Ca2+ release. **Dantrolene**, which acts on RyR1, is the specific treatment. This matters directly to anyone who will put patients under anesthesia.

**Pharmacology and recent advances.** Pharmacologists now target the sarcomere directly. Cardiac myosin modulators established the concept: mavacamten inhibits myosin and omecamtiv mecarbil activates it. Fast skeletal troponin activators such as tirasemtiv and reldesemtiv sensitize the skeletal muscle sarcomere to Ca2+. They have been tested in ALS and SMA, with mixed results. Cryo-electron tomography of intact muscle has resolved the thick filament's OFF state, in which myosin heads fold back onto the filament backbone in the interacting-heads motif. These folded heads are now understood as a reserve that is recruited by strain, a regulatory layer beyond the thin filament.

**Open questions** include how titin senses mechanical strain to drive hypertrophy signaling, and how satellite-cell exhaustion limits regeneration in dystrophies and ageing.

keyPoints: Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated syncytia with peripheral nuclei
A sarcomere runs Z line to Z line: A band (myosin), I band (actin), H zone, M line
In contraction the A band stays constant while the I band and H zone shorten
Triads (T-tubule + two SR cisternae) couple excitation to Ca2+ release via DHPR-RyR1
Ca2+ binds troponin C, moving tropomyosin to expose myosin sites on actin
Titin and nebulin act as molecular spring and ruler; mutations cause myopathies

test.q: Where are the nuclei of a mature skeletal muscle fiber located?
choices: Single and central in each cell
At the periphery under the sarcolemma
test.explain: Skeletal fibers are multinucleated syncytia with nuclei pushed to the edge. A single central nucleus is typical of cardiac and smooth muscle instead.

test.q: A sarcomere is defined as the region between:
test.explain: The sarcomere extends from one Z line (Z disc) to the next.

test.q: During contraction, which band keeps the same width?
test.explain: The A band equals the length of the thick filaments, which do not shorten. The I band and H zone narrow as the filaments slide.

test.q: Which protein anchors thin filaments at the Z disc?
test.explain: Alpha-actinin crosslinks actin barbed ends at the Z disc. Myomesin is found at the M line, not the Z disc.

test.q: A triad in skeletal muscle consists of:
choices: One T-tubule and two SR terminal cisternae
Two T-tubules and one SR terminal cisterna
Three myosin filaments around one actin
One Z disc and two nearby mitochondria
test.explain: A central T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae forms the triad, positioned at the A-I junction in mammals.

test.q: Calcium starts contraction by binding to:
test.explain: Ca2+ binds troponin C, which shifts tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin.

test.q: Which connective tissue layer surrounds each individual muscle fiber?
test.explain: Endomysium surrounds single fibers. Perimysium wraps fascicles and epimysium wraps the whole muscle.

test.q: Type I skeletal muscle fibers are best described as:
test.explain: Type I fibers are slow oxidative, with plenty of myoglobin and mitochondria, which makes them look red.

test.q: What pumps calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum so muscle relaxes?
test.explain: SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the SR. Ryanodine receptors are the channels that release it.

test.q: The thick filaments of the sarcomere are made mainly of the protein ___.
test.explain: Thick filaments are myosin, and thin filaments are mostly actin.

test.q: What name is given to the muscle stem cells lying between the sarcolemma and basal lamina?
test.explain: Satellite cells activate to repair and regenerate damaged fibers.

test.q: The light I band contains only thin filaments made mostly of ___.
test.explain: The I band is the region of thin (actin) filaments not overlapped by myosin.

kidTest.q: What do skeletal muscle fibers look like under a microscope?
kidTest.explain: Repeating sarcomeres give the fibers their stripes.

kidTest.q: What are the tiny repeating boxes inside muscle called?
kidTest.explain: Sarcomeres are the little boxes that shorten to make a muscle pull.

kidTest.q: What happens to the threads when a muscle pulls?
choices: They melt away into the blood
They twist into a tight knot
Thick ones pull thin ones in
kidTest.explain: Thick threads grab the thin threads and pull them in, like pulling a rope.

kidTest.q: Who tells your muscles to move?
kidTest.explain: Your brain sends the signal to move.

kidTest.q: Muscles use an energy molecule to pull. Its name is A _ _.
kidTest.explain: ATP is the fuel that powers muscle pulling.

advancedTest.q: Gordon, Huxley and Julian found that active force falls as sarcomeres are stretched beyond about 2.2 µm. The best explanation is:
choices: Z discs detach from the thin filaments
Calcium release from the SR is inhibited
Titin unfolds and blocks the myosin heads
Fewer myosin heads can reach overlapping actin
advancedTest.explain: Force scales with filament overlap, which sets the number of cross-bridges that can form. Titin generates passive tension rather than blocking myosin heads.

advancedTest.q: With no ATP present after death, muscles stay rigid because myosin:
choices: Fails to bind actin without energy
Pumps calcium back into the SR
advancedTest.explain: ATP binding is what releases myosin from actin. Without it, heads lock in the rigor state.

advancedTest.q: A biopsy shows large patches of fibers that are all the same type. This most likely reflects:
advancedTest.explain: Reinnervating axons convert the fibers they adopt to their own type, which produces fiber-type grouping instead of the normal checkerboard.

advancedTest.q: Why does dantrolene treat malignant hyperthermia?
choices: It stops myosin from hydrolyzing ATP
It blocks the neuromuscular acetylcholine receptor
It reduces uncontrolled Ca2+ release through RyR1
It activates SERCA to speed up relaxation
advancedTest.explain: Malignant hyperthermia involves RYR1-linked uncontrolled SR Ca2+ release. Dantrolene acts on RyR1 to curb it.

lessons.title: Cardiac & Smooth Muscle Compared

levels.kid:
Your body has three kinds of muscle. You already know the kind that moves your arms and legs. Now meet the other two!

**Heart muscle** is in your heart. Its cells are like bricks that hold hands tightly, so they squeeze together all at once. Under a microscope they look striped, a bit like a zebra. Each cell usually has one middle center called a nucleus.

**Smooth muscle** lines tubes inside you, like your stomach, gut and blood vessels. Its cells are shaped like long, skinny rice grains. They have no stripes, so they look smooth. They squeeze slowly and can stay squeezed for a long time.

You do not have to think to use either one. They work all by themselves, day and night.
levels.hs:
Besides skeletal muscle, the body has two **involuntary** muscle types: you do not consciously control them.

**Cardiac muscle** forms the heart wall (the myocardium).
- Cells are **striated** (striped), because their contractile proteins are lined up in repeating units, just like in skeletal muscle.
- Each cell is short and **branched**, with usually one or two **central nuclei**.
- Cells join end to end at **intercalated discs**, dark lines seen on a slide. These contain **gap junctions**, tiny channels that let electrical signals pass straight from cell to cell, so the heart contracts as one unit.
- Cardiac muscle cannot really regrow; after a heart attack, dead muscle is replaced by scar tissue.

**Smooth muscle** is found in the walls of hollow organs: blood vessels, intestines, bladder, uterus and airways.
- Cells are **spindle-shaped** (fat in the middle, tapered at the ends) with one central, often cigar-shaped nucleus.
- They are **not striated**, because their proteins are not arranged in neat rows.
- They contract slowly but can hold a contraction for a long time using little energy.
- They can divide and regenerate fairly well.

Example: in your intestine, two layers of smooth muscle squeeze in waves called **peristalsis**, pushing food along without you ever thinking about it.
levels.college:
Cardiac and smooth muscle are both involuntary, but they differ sharply in structure and control.

**Cardiac muscle (cardiomyocytes)**
- Striated, with sarcomeres like skeletal muscle, but cells are short (roughly 100 µm), branched, and have 1–2 **central nuclei**, often with a pale perinuclear zone holding glycogen and lipofuscin.
- **Intercalated discs** run in a step-like pattern. Their transverse parts hold **fasciae adherentes** (anchoring actin) and **desmosomes** (resisting pulling forces). Their lateral parts hold **gap junctions** made of connexin 43, which electrically couple cells into a functional syncytium.
- T-tubules sit at the **Z line** and pair with sarcoplasmic reticulum as **dyads**, not the triads of skeletal muscle.
- Very rich in mitochondria and aerobic, with no tolerance for oxygen debt.
- **Calcium-induced calcium release**: Ca²⁺ entering through L-type channels triggers ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) on the SR.
- Atrial myocytes contain granules of **atrial natriuretic peptide**.

**Smooth muscle**
- Spindle cells with one central nucleus that can look corkscrew-shaped when contracted. No sarcomeres, no T-tubules; **caveolae** stand in for them.
- Actin thin filaments anchor to **dense bodies** (contain α-actinin, like Z lines) in the cytoplasm and on the membrane.
- Contraction is regulated on myosin, not troponin: Ca²⁺–**calmodulin** activates **myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK)**, which phosphorylates the regulatory light chain.
- **Latch state** keeps tension with low ATP use.
- Cells are joined by gap junctions in **single-unit** (visceral) smooth muscle, such as gut and uterus; **multi-unit** muscle, such as iris and vas deferens, has cells driven individually by nerves.
- Cells secrete their own extracellular matrix and external lamina, and can proliferate.

On H&E, cardiac muscle shows branching striated fibers with discs; smooth muscle shows pink, unstriated sheets of tightly packed spindle cells.
levels.phd:
The molecular logic of each muscle type tracks its functional demand: rhythmic, coordinated pumping versus slow, sustained tone.

**Cardiac excitation–contraction coupling.** Depolarization opens Cav1.2 (L-type) channels in T-tubules, which in ventricle are wide and also run axially. The small trigger Ca²⁺ influx activates closely apposed RyR2 clusters across a dyadic cleft of about 12–15 nm (Fabiato's calcium-induced calcium release). This contrasts with the direct mechanical Cav1.1–RyR1 coupling of skeletal muscle. Relaxation depends on **SERCA2a**, held back by phospholamban, and on the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger. Force is graded by how much Ca²⁺ is released and by sarcomere length (Frank–Starling), not by recruiting more units, because the syncytium fires all-or-none. Gap junctions are concentrated at intercalated discs, with Cx43 in working myocardium and Cx40/Cx45 in conduction tissue. Disc proteins (plakophilin-2, desmoplakin) are now viewed as an integrated **area composita** joining adherens and desmosomal parts.

**Smooth muscle regulation.** Thick filaments are **side-polar**, which allows large shortening. The actin–myosin network inserts obliquely into dense bodies, so contracted cells pucker. Contraction requires phosphorylation of the regulatory light chain at Ser19 by Ca²⁺–calmodulin–MLCK. **Calcium sensitization** occurs through RhoA/ROCK and PKC–CPI-17 inhibition of myosin light-chain phosphatase. Hai and Murphy's latch-bridge model proposed that dephosphorylated cross-bridges detach slowly, holding force cheaply. Thin-filament proteins caldesmon and calponin give additional modulation.

**Plasticity.** Vascular smooth muscle cells shift between contractile and synthetic phenotypes, losing markers such as smooth muscle myosin heavy chain (MYH11) and smoothelin. Lineage tracing (Owens lab) showed SMC-derived cells within atherosclerotic plaques that express macrophage markers. Cardiomyocyte renewal is low: Bergmann et al. (2009), using carbon-14 from Cold War nuclear tests, estimated about 1% per year in young adults, declining with age. Debate continues over claims of resident cardiac stem cells; key c-kit-based papers were retracted.
levels.expert:
Histopathology turns these structural features into clinical reading.

**Cardiac injury timeline.** After infarction, coagulative necrosis with hypereosinophilia and **contraction band necrosis** (in reperfusion) appear within hours. Neutrophils peak at about 1–3 days, macrophages follow, and granulation tissue then collagen scar replace myocytes over weeks. Wavy fibers at the border can be an early clue. Because myocytes barely regenerate, repair is fibrotic, which creates a substrate for re-entrant arrhythmias.

**Disc disease.** Mutations in desmosomal genes (PKP2, DSP, DSG2) cause **arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy**, with fibrofatty replacement, classically in the right ventricle. Gap junction remodeling, in which Cx43 shifts from discs to the lateral membrane, is seen in failing and ischemic hearts and slows conduction. **Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** shows **myocyte disarray** with interstitial fibrosis; sarcomere gene variants (MYH7, MYBPC3) predominate. The cardiac myosin inhibitor mavacamten, which reduces excess actin–myosin cross-bridging, is a mechanism-based therapy now in use.

**Smooth muscle pharmacology** rests on the regulatory pathway. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers relax vascular smooth muscle. Nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors raise cGMP, activating PKG, which promotes myosin light-chain phosphatase activity. ROCK inhibitors (fasudil, netarsudil) target Ca²⁺ sensitization. β2 agonists relax airway smooth muscle; airway smooth muscle hyperplasia and hypertrophy are remodeling features of asthma, and bronchial thermoplasty was developed to ablate this tissue.

**Pitfalls on slides.** Smooth muscle can mimic fibroblasts or nerve. Desmin, smooth muscle actin, h-caldesmon and smooth muscle myosin help, but myofibroblasts also express SMA. Leiomyoma versus leiomyosarcoma depends on mitoses, atypia and tumor necrosis, not on immunostains. Cardiac biopsies are small, and artifactual contraction bands from handling can mimic true necrosis.

**Frontiers.** Human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes stay fetal-like (round, poor T-tubules, immature discs). Maturation via engineered heart tissue and electrical pacing is an active field, as are remuscularization trials using grafts. For neurosurgeons, cerebral vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage is a smooth muscle problem; nimodipine, a calcium channel blocker, improves outcomes there, though its benefit is not clearly explained by angiographic vessel widening alone.

keyPoints: Cardiac muscle: striated, branched cells with 1-2 central nuclei
Intercalated discs join cardiomyocytes with desmosomes, adherens junctions and gap junctions
Smooth muscle: spindle cells, one central nucleus, no striations or sarcomeres
Smooth muscle contraction runs through calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase
Cardiac T-tubules form dyads at the Z line; calcium-induced calcium release
Heart muscle barely regenerates and scars; smooth muscle can divide

test.q: Which feature is unique to cardiac muscle on a slide?
test.explain: Intercalated discs, the step-like junctions between cardiomyocytes, identify cardiac muscle. Dense bodies and spindle cells belong to smooth muscle.

test.q: What lets electrical signals pass directly between cardiac muscle cells?
test.explain: Gap junctions (mainly connexin 43) are channels that electrically couple cells. Desmosomes resist mechanical pulling but do not pass current.

test.q: Why does smooth muscle lack striations?
choices: It takes up special dyes poorly
It contains no actin or myosin
Its filaments are not in sarcomeres
Its nuclei block the light path
test.explain: Smooth muscle has actin and myosin, but they are not lined up in repeating sarcomeres, so no bands appear.

test.q: In smooth muscle, Ca2+ starts contraction by binding to:
test.explain: Ca2+–calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase. Troponin C is the calcium sensor in striated muscle instead.

test.q: Where are nuclei located in cardiac muscle cells?
choices: In clusters at the cell ends
test.explain: Cardiomyocytes have one or two central nuclei. Many peripheral nuclei are typical of skeletal muscle.

test.q: What typically replaces heart muscle that dies after a heart attack?
test.explain: Cardiomyocytes renew very little, so dead myocardium is repaired by fibrous scar.

test.q: Which organ wall is built mainly of smooth muscle?
test.explain: Hollow organs like the bladder have smooth muscle walls. The ventricle is cardiac; diaphragm and tongue are skeletal.

test.q: In cardiac muscle, T-tubules pair with sarcoplasmic reticulum to form:
test.explain: Cardiac muscle forms dyads at the Z line; skeletal muscle forms triads at the A-I junction.

test.q: Single-unit smooth muscle, as in the gut, differs from multi-unit because its cells:
test.explain: Single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle is electrically coupled and contracts as a sheet. Multi-unit cells, like the iris, are driven individually by nerves.

test.q: Smooth muscle can hold tension using little ATP in the ___ state.
test.explain: In the latch state, slowly cycling cross-bridges keep force cheaply.

test.q: What word describes the shape of a smooth muscle cell, fat in the middle and tapered at both ends?
test.explain: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped (fusiform).

test.q: Gut smooth muscle pushes food along in waves called ___.
test.explain: Peristalsis is coordinated, involuntary smooth muscle contraction.

kidTest.q: Where is smooth muscle found?
kidTest.explain: Smooth muscle lines tubes inside you, like your gut and blood vessels.

kidTest.q: What does heart muscle look like under a microscope?
kidTest.explain: Heart muscle is striped, like a zebra.

kidTest.q: What shape are smooth muscle cells?
kidTest.explain: They are long and skinny, tapered at the ends.

kidTest.q: Why do heart cells hold hands tightly?
kidTest.explain: Joining tightly lets them squeeze all at once.

kidTest.q: The muscle with no stripes is called s _ _ _ _ _ muscle.
kidTest.explain: Smooth muscle has no stripes, so it looks smooth.

advancedTest.q: Why can't the heart grade its force by recruiting more motor units, as skeletal muscle does?
choices: Gap junction coupling makes the myocardium fire as one syncytium
Cardiomyocytes lack actin and myosin thick filament overlap
Cardiac T-tubules are missing from ventricular myocytes
The heart has no sarcoplasmic reticulum to store calcium
advancedTest.explain: Electrical coupling makes the heart contract all-or-none, so force is graded by Ca2+ release and sarcomere length instead.

advancedTest.q: A drug inhibiting ROCK would relax smooth muscle mainly by:
choices: Blocking L-type calcium channels in the membrane
Releasing the brake on myosin light-chain phosphatase
Activating troponin to cover myosin binding sites
Stopping calmodulin from being made by the cell
advancedTest.explain: RhoA/ROCK inhibits myosin phosphatase, raising Ca2+ sensitivity; blocking ROCK restores phosphatase activity, so the light chain is dephosphorylated.

advancedTest.q: The carbon-14 study by Bergmann and colleagues most directly showed that:
choices: Smooth muscle cells turn into cardiomyocytes in adults
Adult cardiomyocytes renew at a low, age-declining rate
Cardiomyocytes divide rapidly throughout adult life
Cardiac stem cells rebuild the heart after infarction
advancedTest.explain: Bomb-pulse carbon-14 dating estimated about 1% yearly renewal in young adults, falling with age. Stem cell rebuilding claims were not supported.

advancedTest.q: In a failing heart, Cx43 shifts from intercalated discs to lateral membranes. The likely consequence is:
choices: Conversion of myocytes to smooth muscle
advancedTest.explain: Losing end-to-end gap junctions slows and disorganizes conduction, creating a substrate for re-entrant arrhythmias.

lessons.title: Neurons: Nissl Bodies, Axons & Dendrites

levels.kid:
Your brain is built from tiny cells called **neurons**. They pass messages, like friends whispering down a long line.

Each neuron has three main parts:
- A round **cell body**, the neuron's "house," where the control center lives.
- Many short, bushy **dendrites**, like tree branches, that listen for messages.
- One long **axon**, like a cable, that sends the message on.

Scientists stain neurons with special dyes so they can see them under a microscope. One dye colors little purple dots in the cell body called **Nissl bodies**. These are busy protein factories.

Some axons are very long. One in your leg can reach from your back all the way to your toes!
levels.hs:
A **neuron** is a nerve cell specialized to receive, process and send electrical signals. Under the microscope it has three regions.

- The **cell body** (also called the **soma** or **perikaryon**) holds a large, pale nucleus with a dark, obvious **nucleolus**. Some histologists call this an "owl's eye" look.
- **Dendrites** are short, branching extensions that receive signals from other neurons.
- The **axon** is usually a single long extension that carries signals away from the cell body toward other cells.

With basic dyes such as **cresyl violet** or toluidine blue, the cell body shows purple clumps called **Nissl bodies**. These are stacks of **rough endoplasmic reticulum** packed with ribosomes, which make proteins. Neurons need huge amounts of protein to keep their long processes alive.

Here's a key clue for reading slides: Nissl bodies also extend into dendrites but stop before the axon. The axon starts at a pale, cone-shaped region called the **axon hillock**, which has no Nissl substance.

A real example is the **motor neuron** in the spinal cord's anterior (ventral) horn. It has a huge cell body with coarse Nissl bodies. Its axon travels out to a muscle and can be about a meter long in an adult. Neurons are classified by shape: **multipolar** (many dendrites, one axon), **bipolar**, and **pseudounipolar**.
levels.college:
Neurons are excitable cells whose structure reflects their job of directional signaling. Most are postmitotic, so their maintenance depends on an intensely active cell body.

**Perikaryon.** It has a large euchromatic nucleus, a prominent nucleolus, abundant mitochondria, an extensive Golgi apparatus, and **Nissl substance**. Nissl bodies are rough ER cisternae with polyribosomes. Their RNA is basophilic, so they stain with cresyl violet. Large motor neurons have coarse "tigroid" Nissl bodies. Neurons can also accumulate **lipofuscin**, a "wear-and-tear" pigment, with age.

**Dendrites.** They taper with distance and branch extensively. They contain Nissl substance, Golgi outposts and **MAP2**-associated microtubules of mixed polarity. Many bear **dendritic spines**, the main sites of excitatory synapses. Golgi silver impregnation reveals spines and branching beautifully.

**Axon.** It arises from the **axon hillock**. Next comes the **axon initial segment (AIS)**, which is dense in voltage-gated Na+ channels and is where action potentials usually start. The axon has a uniform diameter. It contains **tau**-associated microtubules with plus ends pointing distally, neurofilaments, smooth ER and mitochondria. It lacks rough ER, so it cannot make most of its own proteins.

**Axonal transport** moves material along microtubules:
- **Anterograde** transport, driven by **kinesin**, carries cargo from soma to terminal. Fast transport moves about 200-400 mm/day; slow transport moves about 1-5 mm/day.
- **Retrograde** transport, driven by **dynein**, carries cargo from terminal to soma, including growth factors and some viruses (rabies, herpes simplex, tetanus toxin).

**Classification by shape:**
- **Multipolar**: motor neurons and pyramidal cells. This is the most common type.
- **Bipolar**: retina and olfactory epithelium.
- **Pseudounipolar**: dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons.

**Chromatolysis** occurs after an axon is cut. The cell body swells, the nucleus moves to the edge, and Nissl bodies disperse. These changes reflect a switch toward making regeneration proteins.
levels.phd:
The neuron doctrine was the product of the **Golgi-Cajal** dispute, for which both men shared the 1906 Nobel Prize. Golgi's silver chromate method sparsely labels about 1-5% of neurons, but it labels each one completely. Cajal used it to argue that neurons are discrete, polarized units, against Golgi's reticular theory. Electron microscopy of the synaptic cleft in the 1950s settled the question. Franz **Nissl** introduced aniline-dye staining in the 1880s-1890s. Cytoarchitectonic maps such as Brodmann's areas rest on that Nissl stain.

**Polarity machinery.** The AIS is organized by **ankyrin-G** and **βIV-spectrin**. These proteins cluster Nav1.6 and Nav1.2 channels, KCNQ2/3 channels and neurofascin-186. Super-resolution microscopy has shown periodic actin-spectrin rings about 190 nm apart along axons. The AIS also acts as a diffusion barrier and a cargo filter that maintains axon-dendrite polarity. If ankyrin-G is lost, axons acquire dendritic features, including spines.

**Microtubule polarity** is the main way cargo gets sorted. Axonal microtubules are uniformly plus-end-out. Mammalian dendrites have mixed orientation, so dynein can carry cargo into dendrites. Kinesin-1 favors axons and kinesin-3 (KIF1A) moves synaptic-vesicle precursors. Signaling endosomes containing TrkA-NGF travel retrogradely by dynein-dynactin to the soma.

**Local translation** changes the old idea that the soma makes everything. Polyribosomes sit at spine bases (Steward and Levy, 1982). Axons, once thought to lack translation, translate mRNAs locally during development and regeneration. Even so, Nissl-defined rough ER remains somatodendritic.

**Chromatolysis** is a phenotype of the axon reaction. It involves ribosomal disaggregation and an injury program driven by retrograde signals such as importin-β and DLK. The program induces regeneration-associated genes, including ATF3, c-Jun and GAP-43. Central neurons mount this response weakly compared with peripheral ones.

**Scale.** A human lower-motor-neuron axon can have a volume of hundreds to thousands of times that of its soma. That size explains why transport defects preferentially damage the longest axons. A neocortical pyramidal cell carries roughly 10^4 spines.
levels.expert:
For the pathologist and neurosurgeon, neuronal morphology is diagnostic.

**Neuronal injury on H&E.** The classic **"red neuron"** of acute ischemia appears about 6-24 hours after injury. It shows a shrunken, hypereosinophilic cytoplasm, loss of Nissl substance and a pyknotic nucleus. The CA1 hippocampal pyramidal cells, Purkinje cells and neocortical layers 3, 5 and 6 are selectively vulnerable.

The main pitfall is the **"dark neuron" artifact**. It comes from handling or delayed fixation of unperfused biopsy tissue and mimics ischemic change. Look for context such as surrounding edema and a reactive response, and do not rely on a single dark cell. Central chromatolysis must also be distinguished from ballooned neurons in corticobasal degeneration and Pick disease, and from storage disorders.

**Inclusions inside neurons:**
- Neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau) in Alzheimer disease.
- Lewy bodies (α-synuclein) in Parkinson disease.
- Negri bodies in rabies, especially in Purkinje cells.
- Bunina bodies and TDP-43 in ALS.

**Neurosurgical pathology.** On intraoperative frozen sections, recognizing dysmorphic neurons is decisive. These cells are disoriented and cytomegalic, with clumped Nissl substance and abnormal neurofilament accumulation. They define focal cortical dysplasia type II, which is often resected for epilepsy, and they also appear in ganglioglioma. Immunostains help confirm neuronal identity: NeuN (Rbfox3), synaptophysin, chromogranin and neurofilament. NeuN is notably negative in Purkinje cells.

**Clinical implications of axon length.** Length-dependent "stocking-glove" neuropathies follow from transport failure in the longest axons. Chemotherapy causes this pattern through vinca alkaloids and taxanes, which disrupt microtubules. KIF5A and DYNC1H1 mutations cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, ALS and SMA-like phenotypes. Retrograde transport is also exploited deliberately. Some gene-therapy approaches target motor neurons through viral vectors such as AAV, including intrathecal routes. Tracers like cholera toxin B map circuits.

**Frontiers.** Three active areas stand out:
- AIS plasticity: activity shifts the length and position of the segment, which matters for epilepsy.
- Expansion microscopy and connectomics: millimeter-scale reconstructions resolving every spine.
- The unresolved question of why adult CNS neurons regenerate so poorly. Intrinsic brakes such as PTEN/mTOR loss compete with extrinsic inhibitors as explanations.

keyPoints: Neurons have a cell body (perikaryon), branching dendrites and usually one axon
Nissl bodies are basophilic rough ER stacks seen with cresyl violet
Nissl substance enters dendrites but is absent from the axon hillock and axon
The axon initial segment, rich in Na+ channels, starts action potentials
Kinesin drives anterograde transport; dynein drives retrograde transport
Neurons are multipolar, bipolar or pseudounipolar; axon injury causes chromatolysis

test.q: What are Nissl bodies made of?
test.explain: Nissl bodies are rough ER cisternae with polyribosomes, and their RNA makes them basophilic. Smooth ER lacks the ribosomes that give the staining.

test.q: Which region of a neuron lacks Nissl substance?
test.explain: The axon hillock and axon contain no rough ER, so they appear pale. This is how you tell the axon from dendrites on a slide.

test.q: Which stain is classically used to show Nissl bodies?
test.explain: Cresyl violet is a basic dye that binds the RNA in Nissl substance. The other stains target collagen, carbohydrates and lipids.

test.q: Which motor protein drives anterograde axonal transport?
test.explain: Kinesin moves cargo toward microtubule plus ends, from soma to terminal. Dynein does the reverse, carrying cargo back to the soma.

test.q: Where are action potentials usually initiated?
choices: The dendritic spines of the neuron
The nucleolus within the cell body
test.explain: The axon initial segment has a high density of voltage-gated Na+ channels, so action potentials usually start there.

test.q: Dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons are classified as:
test.explain: DRG neurons are pseudounipolar: a single process leaves the cell body and splits into a peripheral branch and a central branch. Bipolar neurons, with two separate processes, are found in the retina and olfactory epithelium. Multipolar neurons, such as motor neurons, have many dendrites. Anaxonic neurons, such as some amacrine cells, lack a distinguishable axon.

test.q: What happens to the cell body during chromatolysis after an axon is cut?
choices: It extrudes its nucleus into the space
It swells and its Nissl bodies disperse
It divides into two daughter cells
It shrinks and its Nissl bodies enlarge
test.explain: In chromatolysis the soma swells, the nucleus moves to the edge, and Nissl substance disperses as the cell shifts to making regeneration proteins.

test.q: Dendritic spines are the main sites of:
test.explain: Most excitatory synapses form on dendritic spines. Action potentials start at the axon initial segment instead.

test.q: Which feature describes axons rather than dendrites?
test.explain: Axons keep a uniform diameter and have microtubules that all point plus-end-out. The other features belong to dendrites.

test.q: What is another name for the neuron cell body, starting with 'p'?
test.explain: The perikaryon (soma) contains the nucleus and the Nissl substance.

test.q: Retrograde axonal transport is driven by the motor protein ___.
test.explain: Dynein carries cargo toward the soma, such as growth factors and some viruses.

test.q: What name is given to the age-related wear-and-tear pigment found in neurons?
test.explain: Lipofuscin accumulates in long-lived postmitotic neurons as they age.

kidTest.q: Which part of a neuron listens for messages?
kidTest.explain: Bushy dendrites receive messages, like tree branches catching them.

kidTest.q: Which part sends the message on, like a long cable?
kidTest.explain: The axon carries the message away to the next cell.

kidTest.q: What do Nissl bodies do?
kidTest.explain: Nissl bodies are little protein factories in the cell body.

kidTest.q: How long can one axon in your leg be?
choices: About the size of a sand grain
About as long as your fingernail
From your back to your toes
kidTest.explain: Some axons run all the way from your back down to your toes.

kidTest.q: Brain cells that pass messages are called n _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Neurons are the message-passing cells of your brain and nerves.

advancedTest.q: Genetic loss of ankyrin-G in a neuron would most likely cause:
choices: Nissl bodies appearing within the axon hillock
Conversion of the neuron to a pseudounipolar shape
Axons acquiring dendritic features such as spines
Faster anterograde transport in the axon
advancedTest.explain: Ankyrin-G organizes the AIS barrier that maintains polarity. Without it, axons take on dendritic identity, including spines.

advancedTest.q: Why do dynein-driven cargoes enter mammalian dendrites but not normally travel distally down axons?
choices: Axonal microtubules point minus-end-out, so dynein moves away from soma
Dynein is degraded by proteases concentrated at the axon hillock
Dendrites lack microtubules and move cargo along actin filaments instead
Dendritic tracks have mixed polarity; axonal ones point plus-end-out
advancedTest.explain: Dynein moves toward minus ends. Mixed-polarity dendritic microtubules give it outward-pointing minus ends, while uniform plus-end-out axonal tracks send dynein only toward the soma.

advancedTest.q: A frozen section from unperfused biopsy tissue shows scattered shrunken, dark neurons with no edema or reactive response. The best interpretation is:
choices: Acute ischemic red neurons from a recent infarct
advancedTest.explain: Dark neurons appear when unperfused tissue is handled or fixed late. Without supporting context such as edema or a reactive response, ischemia should not be diagnosed.

advancedTest.q: Microtubule-disrupting chemotherapy produces a stocking-glove neuropathy mainly because:
choices: The longest axons depend most on intact transport over great distances
Dendritic spines in the feet are lost first
Nissl bodies in distal axons are destroyed
Short axons are richer in rough ER and thus more vulnerable
advancedTest.explain: Axons lack rough ER and rely on transport from the soma, so the longest axons fail first. That is why symptoms appear first in the feet and hands.

lessons.title: Glia & Myelin in CNS vs PNS

levels.kid:
Your brain has nerve cells that send messages. But they have helpers too! These helper cells are called **glia**. The word means "glue," because scientists once thought they just held the brain together.

Some glia are like gardeners. They clean up and feed the nerve cells. Some are like guards. They gobble up germs and trash.

Other glia wrap the long wires of nerve cells in a fatty coat called **myelin**. It works like the plastic around a phone charger cable. It helps messages zoom along much faster.

In the brain, one helper can wrap many wires at once, like an octopus. In your arms and legs, each helper wraps just one small piece of one wire, like a sausage roll.
levels.hs:
Neurons get most of the attention, but the nervous system also contains **glia** (neuroglia), support cells that do not fire action potentials the way neurons do. In the **central nervous system (CNS)**, meaning the brain and spinal cord, there are four main types:
- **Astrocytes**: star-shaped cells that support neurons, help control the chemical environment, and help form the **blood-brain barrier**.
- **Oligodendrocytes**: make myelin in the CNS.
- **Microglia**: the brain's immune cells, which eat debris and microbes.
- **Ependymal cells**: line the fluid-filled ventricles and spinal canal.

In the **peripheral nervous system (PNS)**, the nerves outside the brain and cord, the main glia are **Schwann cells**, which make myelin, and **satellite cells**, which surround neuron cell bodies in ganglia.

**Myelin** is a fatty, multilayered wrapping around axons. It insulates them, so the signal jumps between gaps called **nodes of Ranvier**. This is **saltatory conduction**, and it is much faster than conduction along a bare axon.

A key difference: one oligodendrocyte myelinates segments of many axons, but one Schwann cell myelinates a single segment of one axon.

Real example: in **multiple sclerosis**, the immune system attacks CNS myelin. Signals slow or fail, causing vision problems, weakness and numbness.
levels.college:
**Glia** outnumber or roughly equal neurons, depending on the region. Histologically they are recognized mostly by their small nuclei, because routine H&E shows little of their cytoplasm. Special stains or immunohistochemistry reveal their shapes.

**CNS glia:**
- **Astrocytes**: large, pale, oval nuclei. Their processes end in **perivascular end-feet** around capillaries and form the **glia limitans** under the pia. They are identified by **GFAP** (glial fibrillary acidic protein). Protoplasmic astrocytes are found in gray matter; fibrous astrocytes in white matter. They buffer K+, take up glutamate, store glycogen, and form scars (**gliosis**) after injury.
- **Oligodendrocytes**: small, round, dark nuclei, often with a perinuclear clear halo artifact ("fried egg"). Each extends processes that myelinate internodes on many axons, up to about 40 or more.
- **Microglia**: small, elongated, rod-like nuclei. They are derived from yolk-sac macrophage precursors, not neuroectoderm. Markers include Iba1.
- **Ependymal cells**: ciliated cuboidal-to-columnar cells lining the ventricles. Specialized ependyma forms the choroid plexus epithelium, which secretes CSF.

**PNS glia:**
- **Schwann cells** derive from the neural crest. A myelinating Schwann cell wraps one internode of one axon and is covered by a **basal lamina**. Non-myelinating (Remak) Schwann cells embed several small unmyelinated C-fibers in grooves of their cytoplasm.
- **Satellite cells** form a flattened capsule around neuron cell bodies in sensory and autonomic ganglia.

**Myelin structure.** Myelin is compacted plasma membrane spiraled around the axon. It is lipid-rich, so in H&E it is often dissolved, leaving clear rings, the "neurokeratin" network. Osmium or Luxol fast blue stains it. Nodes of Ranvier concentrate voltage-gated Na+ channels, enabling saltatory conduction.

**Clinical contrast.** Multiple sclerosis destroys CNS myelin made by oligodendrocytes. **Guillain-Barré syndrome** attacks PNS myelin made by Schwann cells. PNS axons regenerate far better than CNS axons.
levels.phd:
Compact myelin forms when cytoplasm is extruded and membrane leaflets fuse. Electron microscopy shows a periodicity of roughly 12 nm. The **major dense line** is the fused cytoplasmic faces; the **intraperiod line** is the apposed extracellular faces. Myelin is about 70-80% lipid, enriched in cholesterol, galactocerebroside and sulfatide. Its protein composition differs between the CNS and PNS:
- **CNS**: proteolipid protein (**PLP**, the most abundant), myelin basic protein (**MBP**), and MOG and MAG.
- **PNS**: protein zero (**P0**, about half the protein, an adhesive Ig-superfamily molecule), PMP22, MBP, and periaxin.

PNS myelin retains cytoplasmic channels called **Schmidt-Lanterman incisures** and a cytoplasm-filled outer collar. Its nodes are covered by Schwann cell microvilli. CNS nodes are instead contacted by perinodal astrocyte processes and are bare of basal lamina.

The node is a molecular mosaic:
- **Node proper**: Nav1.6 clustered by ankyrin-G and betaIV-spectrin.
- **Paranode**: septate-like junctions between axonal Caspr/contactin and glial neurofascin-155.
- **Juxtaparanode**: Kv1 channels.

Myelination is regulated by axonal signals. In the PNS, axonal **neuregulin-1 type III** level determines whether a Schwann cell myelinates and how thickly. Axon diameter predicts myelination fate; the g-ratio (axon diameter divided by fiber diameter) is near 0.6-0.7, close to the theoretical optimum for conduction velocity. The transcription factors are different: Schwann cells depend on **Sox10 and Krox20 (Egr2)**, while oligodendrocytes depend on Olig2, Sox10 and Myrf.

Gene dosage shows how sensitive myelin is. Duplication of **PMP22** causes Charcot-Marie-Tooth 1A, and deletion causes hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies. PLP1 duplication causes Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease.

Regeneration differs sharply. After transection, Schwann cells dedifferentiate into repair cells (c-Jun dependent), clear myelin with macrophages, and form **bands of Büngner** that guide regrowth. CNS myelin debris contains inhibitors such as Nogo-A, MAG and OMgp, and reactive astrocytes form a chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan-rich scar. Aguayo's classic peripheral nerve graft experiments showed that CNS axons can regrow in a permissive environment, so the barrier is largely environmental rather than intrinsic alone.
levels.expert:
For a future neurosurgeon, glial histology matters most in tumor pathology, demyelination and nerve repair.

**Glioma diagnosis** is now integrated and molecular (WHO CNS5, 2021). Morphology alone is unreliable: the "fried egg" halo of oligodendroglioma is a fixation artifact, and frozen sections often lack it. The key molecular markers are:
- **Oligodendroglioma**: IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted.
- **Astrocytoma**: IDH-mutant, typically with ATRX loss and TP53 mutation; CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion raises the grade.
- **Glioblastoma**: IDH-wildtype. Molecular features such as TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification or +7/−10 qualify it even without necrosis or microvascular proliferation.

GFAP and Olig2 confirm glial lineage. Schwannomas, by contrast, are S100- and SOX10-positive. They show Antoni A areas with Verocay bodies and looser Antoni B areas, and typically lose merlin from NF2.

**Pitfalls.** Reactive gliosis can mimic low-grade astrocytoma in a small biopsy. Tumefactive demyelination can mimic a high-grade tumor on MRI, with ring enhancement; the open ring is a clue. Histologically it shows sheets of foamy macrophages and Creutzfeldt cells. CD68 immunostaining and stains for myelin loss with relative axonal preservation (neurofilament) prevent unnecessary resection.

**Demyelination.** Antibody testing now separates MOG antibody-associated disease and aquaporin-4 neuromyelitis optica (an astrocytopathy) from MS, with different prognoses and treatments. Remyelination occurs from **oligodendrocyte precursor cells** (NG2+/PDGFRα+). In chronic MS, however, recruited OPCs often fail to differentiate. Clemastine produced modest latency improvements in the ReBUILD trial, and remyelination remains an unmet goal. Smoldering "slowly expanding" lesions with iron-rim microglia are a current focus.

**Peripheral repair.** Gap length and time are decisive because repair Schwann cells lose capacity and target muscle atrophies over months. Conduits, processed allografts and nerve transfers exploit Schwann cell guidance.

**Open questions** include **adaptive myelination**, the activity-dependent remodeling of myelin that is linked to learning, and astrocyte heterogeneity, including whether reactive "A1/A2" states are a valid classification. Another is glymphatic clearance via astrocytic AQP4, which remains debated.

keyPoints: Glia are non-signaling support cells of the nervous system
CNS glia: astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells
PNS glia: Schwann cells and satellite cells
One oligodendrocyte myelinates many axons; one Schwann cell myelinates one internode
Myelin enables saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier
MS attacks CNS myelin; Guillain-Barré attacks PNS myelin

test.q: Which cell makes myelin in the central nervous system?
test.explain: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons. Schwann cells are the myelinating cells of the PNS.

test.q: A key structural difference between oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells is that:
choices: Schwann cells myelinate many axons each
Schwann cells lack any compact myelin
Oligodendrocytes are covered by basal lamina
test.explain: An oligodendrocyte myelinates segments of many axons, while a myelinating Schwann cell wraps one internode of a single axon.

test.q: Which glial cell is the resident immune cell of the brain?
test.explain: Microglia are macrophage-like cells that remove debris and microbes. Unlike other glia, they derive from yolk-sac precursors.

test.q: GFAP immunostaining is used to identify:
test.explain: Glial fibrillary acidic protein is the classic astrocyte marker.

test.q: Where are ependymal cells found?
test.explain: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal. Satellite cells are the ones that surround ganglion neurons.

test.q: Saltatory conduction is possible because voltage-gated Na+ channels are concentrated at:
test.explain: Action potentials regenerate at the nodes of Ranvier, so the signal jumps from node to node.

test.q: Guillain-Barré syndrome mainly damages myelin made by:
test.explain: Guillain-Barré attacks peripheral myelin, which is made by Schwann cells. MS targets oligodendrocyte (CNS) myelin.

test.q: In routine H&E sections, oligodendrocytes often appear as:
choices: Large cells with blue Nissl bodies
Round nuclei with a clear perinuclear halo
test.explain: The 'fried egg' clear halo around a small round nucleus is a fixation artifact typical of oligodendrocytes.

test.q: Why do peripheral axons regenerate better than CNS axons?
choices: Schwann cells form guiding bands of Büngner
CNS neurons have no axons to regrow
test.explain: Repair Schwann cells clear debris and form bands of Büngner that guide regrowth. CNS myelin inhibitors and astrocytic scars instead hinder CNS regrowth.

test.q: Flattened glial cells that surround neuron cell bodies in ganglia are called ___ cells.
test.explain: Satellite cells form a capsule around neuron cell bodies in sensory and autonomic ganglia.

test.q: What is the name of the fast, node-to-node conduction along myelinated axons?
test.explain: Saltatory comes from the Latin for 'to jump': the signal jumps between nodes.

test.q: Astrocytes help form the blood-brain ___.
test.explain: Astrocytic end-feet surround capillaries and contribute to the blood-brain barrier.

kidTest.q: What does the word 'glia' mean?
kidTest.explain: Scientists once thought glia just glued the brain together.

kidTest.q: What does myelin do for nerve wires?
kidTest.explain: Myelin coats the wire so messages zoom along faster.

kidTest.q: Myelin is most like which everyday thing?
kidTest.explain: Like a cable's plastic coat, myelin insulates the nerve wire.

kidTest.q: Some glia act like guards. What do they do?
kidTest.explain: These guard glia clean up germs and trash in the brain.

kidTest.q: The fatty coat on nerve wires is called m _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Myelin is the fatty wrapping that speeds up messages.

advancedTest.q: A nerve biopsy shows myelin with Schmidt-Lanterman incisures, a basal lamina and abundant P0 protein. This tissue is most likely:
advancedTest.explain: Incisures, basal lamina and P0 are features of Schwann cell (PNS) myelin. The other options are all CNS tracts, where myelin is made by oligodendrocytes and relies on PLP.

advancedTest.q: Charcot-Marie-Tooth 1A and hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies both involve PMP22. What does this imply?
choices: PMP22 builds the nodal Na+ channel complex
PMP22 acts mainly in CNS oligodendrocytes
PMP22 mutations cause demyelination by infection
Myelin depends on correct PMP22 gene dosage
advancedTest.explain: Duplication causes CMT1A and deletion causes HNPP. Both too much and too little PMP22 disrupt PNS myelin, so its gene dosage is critical.

advancedTest.q: Aguayo's peripheral nerve graft experiments suggested that poor CNS axon regeneration is largely due to:
choices: Excess Schwann cells within the brain
Absence of nodes of Ranvier in CNS axons
The inhibitory CNS environment around axons
Intrinsic inability of CNS neurons to grow axons
advancedTest.explain: CNS axons regrew into permissive peripheral grafts. This implicates environmental inhibitors such as Nogo-A, MAG and the astrocytic scar.

advancedTest.q: A ring-enhancing brain lesion on biopsy shows sheets of CD68+ foamy cells, myelin loss with preserved neurofilament staining, and Creutzfeldt cells. The best interpretation is:
advancedTest.explain: Macrophage-rich myelin loss with relatively preserved axons and Creutzfeldt cells indicates tumefactive demyelination. Recognizing it avoids unnecessary resection.

lessons.title: Peripheral Nerves, Ganglia & the Neuromuscular Junction

levels.kid:
Your body has long wires called **nerves**. They carry messages from your brain to your muscles, and from your skin back to your brain.

A nerve is like a big cable stuffed with many tiny wires. Each tiny wire is wrapped in its own cover. Bundles of wires get another cover, and the whole cable gets a tough outer coat. That keeps everything safe when you bend and stretch.

Along the way there are little lumps called **ganglia**. They are like small post offices full of nerve cell bodies.

Where a nerve touches a muscle, there is a special meeting spot. The nerve squirts out a tiny chemical messenger. The muscle feels it and squeezes. That is how you wiggle your toes!
levels.hs:
A **peripheral nerve** is a bundle of axons outside the brain and spinal cord. Under the microscope it has three layers of connective tissue wrapping:

- **Endoneurium**: delicate tissue around each single axon and its Schwann cell.
- **Perineurium**: a sheath of flattened cells around each bundle, called a **fascicle**. Its cells are joined by tight junctions, forming a blood-nerve barrier.
- **Epineurium**: thick, dense outer layer around the whole nerve, containing fat and blood vessels.

On a slide stained with H&E, cut along its length, a nerve looks wavy and pale pink. Myelin looks like empty-looking spaces, because the fatty myelin dissolves during processing.

**Ganglia** are clusters of neuron cell bodies outside the central nervous system. **Sensory ganglia**, such as the dorsal root ganglia, have big round cell bodies, each surrounded by a ring of small **satellite cells**. **Autonomic ganglia** have smaller, more scattered neurons.

The **neuromuscular junction (NMJ)** is the synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber. The nerve ending releases **acetylcholine**, which binds receptors on the muscle and triggers contraction.

Real example: in **myasthenia gravis**, antibodies attack these acetylcholine receptors. Muscles weaken with use, often starting with drooping eyelids.
levels.college:
**Nerve architecture.** Peripheral nerves contain myelinated and unmyelinated axons, Schwann cells, fibroblasts and vessels, organized by three connective tissue compartments:
- **Epineurium**: dense irregular collagen, adipose tissue, vasa nervorum. It cushions the nerve and makes up much of its cross-section.
- **Perineurium**: concentric layers of flattened **perineurial cells** with tight junctions and basal laminae. It is the main diffusion barrier and gives the nerve tensile strength.
- **Endoneurium**: loose reticular and collagen fibers around individual Schwann cell-axon units.

In cross-section, myelinated axons look like a central dot (the axon) inside a pale halo (extracted myelin), with Schwann cell nuclei at the edge. **Osmium tetroxide** preserves myelin as black rings. Longitudinal sections show the wavy course and **nodes of Ranvier**.

**Ganglia.**
- **Sensory ganglia** (dorsal root, trigeminal): large **pseudounipolar** neurons with central nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Each is tightly wrapped by satellite cells. There are no synapses inside.
- **Autonomic ganglia** (sympathetic chain, parasympathetic ganglia in organ walls): smaller **multipolar** neurons with eccentric nuclei and fewer satellite cells. Preganglionic fibers synapse here.

**Neuromuscular junction.**
- The motor axon loses its myelin and branches into terminal **boutons** lying in grooves on the muscle fiber.
- Boutons contain synaptic vesicles of acetylcholine (ACh) and many mitochondria.
- The **synaptic cleft** is about 50 nm wide and contains basal lamina with **acetylcholinesterase**.
- The postsynaptic membrane forms **junctional folds**. Nicotinic ACh receptors cluster at the fold crests. Voltage-gated Na+ channels sit in the troughs.

The sequence: an action potential opens P/Q-type Ca2+ channels, vesicles fuse, ACh binds nicotinic receptors, and the end-plate depolarizes. This triggers a muscle action potential. Acetylcholinesterase ends the signal by breaking ACh down into acetate and choline.
levels.phd:
**Barrier biology.** The perineurium and endoneurial microvessels together form the **blood-nerve barrier**. Perineurial cells express claudin-1, ZO-1 and GLUT1. The barrier is leakier at nerve roots and in ganglia, where capillaries are fenestrated. This partly explains why dorsal root ganglia are vulnerable to circulating toxins and chemotherapy agents such as cisplatin and paclitaxel, producing sensory neuronopathies. Endoneurial fluid is kept at slightly positive pressure. Entrapment and edema can therefore raise it and cause ischemia.

**Quantal transmission.** Katz, del Castillo and Fatt showed in the 1950s that ACh is released in **quanta**. Spontaneous miniature end-plate potentials of about 0.5–1 mV correspond to single vesicles, each holding several thousand ACh molecules. A nerve impulse releases tens to hundreds of quanta. This gives a **safety factor**: the end-plate potential exceeds threshold by several-fold. Heuser and Reese's freeze-fracture and quick-freeze studies showed that vesicles fuse at **active zones** aligned opposite the junctional fold crests. Their work also showed vesicle recycling by endocytosis.

**Receptor clustering.** Postsynaptic organization depends on **agrin**, released by the nerve. Agrin binds **LRP4**, which activates the kinase **MuSK**. Signals through DOK7 then direct **rapsyn** to anchor nicotinic receptors at densities near 10,000/µm². Adult receptors are α2βδε pentamers. The fetal γ subunit replaces ε in development and reappears after denervation, when receptors spread across the whole fiber.

**Disease mapping onto structure.**
- **Myasthenia gravis**: antibodies against AChR (about 85%), MuSK or LRP4. Complement destroys the folds and lowers the safety factor.
- **Lambert-Eaton syndrome**: antibodies to presynaptic P/Q Ca2+ channels, often paraneoplastic with small-cell lung cancer. Strength improves briefly with repeated effort.
- **Botulinum toxin** cleaves SNARE proteins (SNAP-25, synaptobrevin, syntaxin) and blocks exocytosis.
- **α-bungarotoxin** binds AChR almost irreversibly. Labeled versions are the classic tool for imaging end-plates.

A debated point is how much perisynaptic (terminal) Schwann cells actively shape transmission rather than simply guiding repair.
levels.expert:
**Reading nerve biopsies.** Sural nerve biopsy is still used in suspected vasculitic neuropathy, amyloidosis and some inflammatory neuropathies. Semithin resin sections stained with **toluidine blue** are the workhorse. Look for these features:
- **Axonal degeneration**: myelin ovoids and loss of large fibers. Regenerating clusters appear later.
- **Demyelination**: thinly myelinated axons relative to their caliber. Chronic cycles of demyelination and repair produce **onion bulbs**, concentric Schwann cell layers seen in CIDP and Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1.
- **Vasculitis**: inflammation of epineurial vessel walls, sometimes with fibrinoid necrosis. Sampling error is common.
- **Amyloid**: Congo red apple-green birefringence. Transthyretin amyloidosis is now treatable with TTR stabilizers and gene silencers, which raises the stakes of diagnosis.

**Skin punch biopsy** with PGP9.5 immunostaining measures intraepidermal nerve fiber density. It has largely replaced nerve biopsy for diagnosing small-fiber neuropathy.

**Surgical relevance.** Seddon and Sunderland grade nerve injuries by which sheath is disrupted:
- **Neurapraxia**: conduction block with intact axons.
- **Axonotmesis**: axons are cut, but the endoneurial tubes guide regrowth at roughly 1 mm/day.
- **Neurotmesis**: the whole nerve is transected.

Surgeons perform epineurial or group-fascicular repair. Tension-free coaptation and fascicle alignment matter. Gaps need autografts, such as sural nerve, or processed allografts. Nerve transfers rely on reinnervating motor end-plates before they degrade, typically within about 12–18 months. After that, end-plates and muscle fibers undergo irreversible fibrosis.

**NMJ therapeutics and pitfalls.**
- Complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan) and FcRn blockers (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab) have transformed AChR-antibody myasthenia.
- MuSK myasthenia responds poorly to cholinesterase inhibitors but well to rituximab.
- Denervated muscle spreads extrajunctional receptors, including the fetal γ type. Succinylcholine can then cause dangerous hyperkalemia, for example in burns, immobilization or after spinal cord injury.

**Open questions** include why repair often fails in proximal injuries, and whether the repair Schwann cell phenotype (driven by c-Jun) can be prolonged to keep regrowth pathways open.

keyPoints: Peripheral nerves have three wrappings: endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium
The perineurium's tight-junctioned cells form the blood-nerve barrier
Sensory ganglia: large pseudounipolar neurons ringed by satellite cells, no synapses
Autonomic ganglia: smaller multipolar neurons where preganglionic fibers synapse
NMJ: ACh vesicles, a cleft with acetylcholinesterase, junctional folds with nicotinic receptors
Myasthenia gravis targets postsynaptic receptors; Lambert-Eaton targets presynaptic Ca2+ channels

test.q: Which connective tissue layer surrounds a single fascicle of a peripheral nerve?
test.explain: The perineurium wraps each fascicle. Endoneurium surrounds individual axons, and epineurium covers the whole nerve.

test.q: What makes the perineurium an effective diffusion barrier?
choices: Flattened cells joined by tight junctions
A dense layer of adipose cells
test.explain: Perineurial cells are linked by tight junctions, which forms the blood-nerve barrier.

test.q: In a routine H&E section, myelin around axons usually appears:
test.explain: Lipid-rich myelin dissolves during processing, so it looks pale. Osmium tetroxide is the stain that preserves it as black rings.

test.q: Which feature best identifies a dorsal root ganglion?
choices: Rows of neurons separated by junctional folds
Small multipolar neurons with eccentric nuclei
Clusters of neurons inside an organ wall
Large round neurons ringed by satellite cells
test.explain: Sensory ganglia contain large pseudounipolar neurons, each tightly surrounded by satellite cells.

test.q: Where do preganglionic fibers synapse onto other neurons?
test.explain: Autonomic ganglia are relay stations for preganglionic fibers. Sensory ganglia have no synapses inside.

test.q: Which enzyme in the synaptic cleft ends the signal at the neuromuscular junction?
test.explain: Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft basal lamina breaks ACh down into acetate and choline. Choline acetyltransferase makes ACh rather than breaking it down.

test.q: Junctional folds on the muscle side of the NMJ have which arrangement?
choices: ACh receptors at crests, Na+ channels in troughs
Na+ channels at crests, ACh receptors in troughs
Vesicles at crests, mitochondria in troughs
Ca2+ channels at crests, K+ channels in troughs
test.explain: Nicotinic receptors cluster at fold crests facing release sites. Voltage-gated Na+ channels in the troughs amplify depolarization.

test.q: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies most often attack:
test.explain: Myasthenia gravis targets postsynaptic ACh receptors. Antibodies to presynaptic Ca2+ channels cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome instead.

test.q: Which entry of Ca2+ triggers vesicle release at the motor nerve terminal?
test.explain: The action potential opens presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, which triggers vesicle fusion.

test.q: The bundle of axons wrapped by perineurium is called a ___.
test.explain: Fascicles are the bundles inside a nerve, each wrapped by perineurium.

test.q: Which neurotransmitter is released at the skeletal neuromuscular junction?
test.explain: Motor neurons release acetylcholine, which acts on nicotinic receptors.

test.q: The small cells that ring each neuron in a sensory ganglion are called ___ cells.
test.explain: Satellite cells are glia that tightly surround ganglion neuron cell bodies.

kidTest.q: What do nerves do?
kidTest.explain: Nerves carry messages between the brain and the body.

kidTest.q: A nerve is most like:
choices: A cable full of tiny wires
kidTest.explain: A nerve holds many tiny wires bundled together inside covers.

kidTest.q: What are ganglia?
kidTest.explain: Ganglia are little clusters of nerve cell bodies, like small post offices.

kidTest.q: What happens when a nerve sends its chemical to a muscle?
kidTest.explain: The chemical messenger makes the muscle contract, or squeeze.

kidTest.q: Long body wires that carry messages are called n _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Nerves carry messages to and from the brain.

advancedTest.q: Why are dorsal root ganglia especially vulnerable to some chemotherapy agents?
choices: Their satellite cells actively pump drugs into neurons
Their perineurium is replaced there by thick adipose tissue
Their neurons have too few mitochondria to detoxify drugs
Their fenestrated capillaries weaken the blood-nerve barrier
advancedTest.explain: The blood-nerve barrier is leakier in ganglia because the capillaries are fenestrated. This exposes the neuron cell bodies to circulating toxins.

advancedTest.q: A patient's weakness briefly improves with repeated effort. Which lesion fits best?
choices: Cleavage of SNARE proteins by a toxin
advancedTest.explain: In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, repeated activity builds up presynaptic Ca2+ and boosts release. Myasthenia gravis typically worsens with use.

advancedTest.q: Why does axonotmesis usually recover better than neurotmesis?
choices: It spares the motor end-plates from any denervation
It does not trigger Wallerian degeneration distally
Its endoneurial tubes stay intact and guide regrowth
Its axons remain fully intact across the lesion
advancedTest.explain: In axonotmesis the axons are cut, but the connective tissue sheaths survive and guide regenerating axons back to their targets.

advancedTest.q: Why can succinylcholine cause hyperkalemia after prolonged denervation?
choices: Acetylcholinesterase activity rises far above normal
Schwann cells release potassium when they are activated
Receptors spread across the fiber, including fetal γ types
Junctional folds deepen and trap potassium in the cleft
advancedTest.explain: Denervated muscle expresses extrajunctional receptors across the whole membrane, so a depolarizing drug opens many more channels and releases more potassium.
